messages.author: e5c7e56038437512
messages.subject: SPDE method in TMB
parts:
Hi!

Well, I was reviewing the implementation of the spde method here:
https://kaskr.github.io/adcomp/R__inla_8hpp_source.html
where Q is calculated as follows:
Q = kappa^4*M0 + 2*kappa^2*M0 + M1

but, in this article https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.06350.pdf, equation 16, the mathematical expression for Q is:
Q = tau^2(kappa^4*M0 + 2*kappa^2*M0 + M1)

Probably, if you fix tau = 1, then it should not be a problem when you are doing frequentist inference, but what happens if you want to do Bayesian inference with tmbstan? "tau" in this case could has implications in the convergence of the chains. 

Cheers!

messages.author: aaa2ae7e32b31e22
messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] SPDE method in TMB
parts: I'm not sure that this is the best venue for discussing, but (if I remember right) kappa is the decorrelation rate per unit distance and 1/tau^2 is proportional the variance per unit distance.  The pointwise (a.k.a. marginal) variance is  then (I think) 1 / sqrt(2*pi * kappa^2 * tau^2) and the decorrelation range is sqrt(8)/kappa.  With infill asymptotics, the tau is often well-defined and asymptotically consistent while kappa is not ... hence using a kappa-variance parameterization results in neither parameter (kappa or variance) being well-behaved using infill asymptotics, which is why INLA typically uses the kappa-tau parameterization instead.  Calculating Q without tau (your first equation) is in some sense the "centered" parameterization, and it then requires scaling the random effect by 1/tau later in the model.  Calculating Q with tau (your second equation) is in some sense the "noncentered" parameterization, and it does not require transforming the random effect later.  Whether the centered or noncentered converges faster in MLE or Bayesian mixing depends on the amount of information.

messages.author: e5c7e56038437512
messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] SPDE method in TMB
parts:
Hi!

Thanks for your answers!

Jim: If you are referring to scale the spatial random effect as:
nll_u += SCALE(GMRF(Q), 1/tau)(u);  //             where u is the spatial random effect

then there are lot of problems to achieve the convergence in the chains. Indeed, if a leave the model only as:
nll_u += GMRF(Q)(u);   

then the last one work much better than the first one parameterization. So, in this case, we have big differences (estimation and computational efficiency) between those two parametrization when we are doing Bayesian inference. 

Hans: Yeah, as I commented before, there are no problems when you are using the Laplace approximation for the estimations under the frequentist approach. 
So, I tried using your equation:
mu = Xbeta + u(site)/tau;

and I have the same problems. 

Please, consider that I was talking about the parametrization of the spde method using "R_inla" namespace. 

Now I will try calculating

as an embedded function in the c++ template. 
Cheers,

El domingo, 14 de mayo de 2023 a las 15:48:22 UTC+2, Hans Skaug escribió:
The two formulations (using code from the spde.cpp example):
1)
Q = kappa^4*M0 + 2*kappa^2*M0 + M1
Type eta = Xbeta(i) + x(meshidxloc(i))/tau;

2)
Q = tau^2(kappa^4*M0 + 2*kappa^2*M0 + M1)
Type eta = Xbeta(i) + x(meshidxloc(i));

are mathematically identical (modulo some numerical issues maybe),
in the sense that the likelihood after applying the Laplace approximation
(wrt x) is the same.

I assume that you plan to apply tmbstan to the hyperparameters (not x),
and it that case it should not matter much which formulation you choose.
